Calcite. Calcium carbonate, a mineral found everywhere—in sedimentary rocks, metamorphic rocks, and even igneous rocks. It forms the primary constituent of limestone and marble, and it's crucial to coral reefs and the shells of molluscs. Its softness, its tendency to dissolve in acid, and its habit of forming crystals make it highly recognisable in the field.

Calcite is rated just three on the Mohs hardness scale, which means it's soft enough to scratch with a knife—much softer than quartz or feldspar. One of the easiest ways to identify it is that it fizzes when you expose it to dilute hydrochloric acid. It forms beautiful rhombohedral crystals, those three-sided diamond shapes. The transparent varieties, sometimes called Iceland spar, have been used as optical elements.

The primary mineral in limestone, a sedimentary rock, and in marble, which is metamorphic limestone that's been transformed by burial and heat. Much of the calcite in nature has a biogenic origin—it precipitates from seawater through the activity of organisms like corals, foraminifera, and molluscs, rather than crystallising inorganically. The solubility of calcite in acidic water means that limestone landscapes develop karst topography: caves, sinkholes, underground rivers, and dramatic cliff formations.

Limestone is calcite-rich sedimentary rock formed from shell fragments and skeletal material from ancient seas. Marble forms when limestone is metamorphosed under heat and pressure, causing the calcite crystals to grow larger and recrystallise. Calcite sits at the lower end of the Mohs hardness scale, and it's one of the few minerals persistent enough to break down quartz chemically over time.
